# In the Margins

There's a manuscript in the archives of Dubrovnik, a dull administrative record from the 1400s, with four inky paw prints marching across one page. Some cat walked through a spilled inkwell and then across the work. Nobody scraped them off, and nobody recopied the page. The prints just stayed, and now, five centuries later, they're the most famous thing about the document.

I think about that cat more than I should, because it points at something I find quietly moving: the best parts of old books are often the parts nobody meant to keep.

Medieval scribes spent their lives copying texts they didn't write, in handwriting meant to be anonymous and uniform. But in the margins, they leaked. One Irish monk scrawled beside his work: *"Thank God, it will soon be dark."* Another: *"New parchment, bad ink. I say nothing more."* Someone else complained that his hand was tired, or that the cold was terrible, or noted, apropos of nothing, that a blackbird was singing outside. These are the lines that survive in the popular imagination. Not the sacred text, which was copied a thousand times, but the one-off grumble of a man with cold fingers who wanted to go to bed.

It's a little humbling. You labor over the official thing, and what reaches the future is your sigh.

---

Marginalia turn reading into a conversation, though a strange, lopsided one. The author has said their piece and can't respond. The annotator talks back anyway: *No. Wrong. Yes!! See p. 40. Ridiculous.* Mark Twain filled the margins of books he disliked with withering commentary, as if the author might someday check. Coleridge annotated so prolifically, often in books borrowed from friends, that his marginal notes were eventually collected and published in several volumes. His friends reportedly came to value the books more *because* he'd defaced them.

And then there's Fermat, who in 1637 wrote in the margin of an ancient Greek math text that he had found a truly marvelous proof of a certain proposition, which this margin was too narrow to contain. That scribble cost mathematicians roughly 358 years. Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in the 1990s, using mathematics Fermat couldn't possibly have had, which suggests Fermat's "marvelous proof" was probably mistaken. The most consequential margin note in history may have been a man being briefly, confidently wrong in a space too small to check his work.

I find that oddly comforting. The margin is where you're allowed to be unfinished.

---

What I love about all this is that marginalia reveal reading as something *active*. We tend to picture reading as reception: words flow in, the reader absorbs. But the margins show people arguing, underlining, making connections the author never intended, drawing tiny hands pointing at important lines (medieval readers did this so often the symbol has a name: the manicule ☞). A book with marginalia is a record of a mind colliding with another mind. Two people across time, one of them talking and one of them interrupting.

Used bookstores sometimes sell annotated copies at a discount, as though the notes were damage. I understand why; if you want a clean text, a stranger's opinions are clutter. But I've always thought it's backwards. A clean copy has one voice in it. An annotated copy has at least two, sometimes more, when a book passes through several owners, each adding a layer in different ink, occasionally responding to each other. *"This is the best chapter"* in pencil, and underneath, decades later, in blue ballpoint: *"It really isn't."*

That's not damage. That's a thread.

---

I suppose I'm drawn to this because so much of what's precious about people lives in the unofficial register. The eulogy lists accomplishments, but the people in the room are remembering how she hummed while cooking, or the specific way he mispronounced a word on purpose for thirty years because it once made someone laugh. The résumé is the text; the life is in the margins.

The cat didn't mean anything by it. The monk just wanted it to be dark. Fermat just wanted to jot something down before he forgot. None of them were trying to be remembered, which may be exactly why they were.

So if you have a book you love, I'd gently suggest writing in it. Argue with it. Note the date you read it and where you were. Someday someone else might pick it up and find you there, a little unfinished, talking back, leaving paw prints across the page.

I have full creative freedom here, so I want to pick a topic that feels genuinely interesting rather than obvious — something like the drift of words like "nice" over time, or the small pleasure in things that are slightly imperfect. I'm leaning toward writing an essay around one of these threads.

Actually I think marginalia is the richer subject: centuries of readers scribbling to dead authors, Fermat's famous note in the margin, Coleridge's annotations, medieval scribes grumbling about bad ink, even a cat's paw prints on an old manuscript. I want to weave these true details into a warm, moderate-length reflection on that long, quiet conversation between readers and writers.
